title: Seller Property Disclosure Statement (Customary — Caveat Emptor State)
description: Montana is largely a caveat emptor state: no statute requires a general seller property condition disclosure form for residential resales. The Montana Association of REALTORS Property Disclosure Statement is customary and strongly recommended to reduce liability, but it is not statutorily mandated. Note, however, that real estate licensees have an independent statutory duty under Mont. Code Ann. § 37-51-313 to disclose known adverse material facts concerning the property to the buyer, and common-law fraud/misrepresentation liability still applies to sellers who actively conceal defects.

required_actions.note: Montana Association of REALTORS Property Disclosure Statement — customary, not statutory.

Caveat emptor posture: seller has no general statutory disclosure duty, but licensees must disclose known adverse material facts (Mont. Code Ann. § 37-51-313) and sellers remain liable for fraudulent concealment.

citations: Mont. Code Ann. § 37-51-102 (adverse material fact definition)

title: Mold Disclosure (Montana Mold Disclosure Act)
description: Under the Montana Mold Disclosure Act, Mont. Code Ann. § 70-16-703, a seller or seller's agent who has knowledge that a building has mold present must disclose the presence of mold to the buyer prior to or upon entry into the purchase contract, and must disclose the results of any prior mold testing on request. Providing the statutory mold disclosure statement (with the prescribed warning language) on a transaction document signed by the buyer confers immunity from liability for mold-based claims, so the disclosure statement is standard on Montana Buy-Sell Agreements.

required_actions.note: Disclose known mold presence to buyer prior to or upon contract; disclose prior mold testing results on request.
Statutory mold disclosure statement; buyer acknowledges receipt by signature. Compliance confers statutory immunity from mold-based liability.

title: Noxious Weed Disclosure on Sale of Land
description: Mont. Code Ann. § 7-22-2116 (County Noxious Weed Control Act) makes it unlawful to permit noxious weeds to propagate or go to seed and requires that when property is offered for sale, the owner notify the owner's agent and the purchaser of (a) the existence of noxious weed infestations on the property and (b) the existence of any noxious weed management program or noxious weed management agreement covering the property. This is most significant for rural, agricultural, and unplatted land, where the buyer inherits the statutory weed-control duty owed to the county weed district.

required_actions.note: Seller must notify agent and purchaser of noxious weed infestations and any weed management program or agreement (Mont. Code Ann. § 7-22-2116(2)).
Buyer assumes the landowner duty to control noxious weeds under the county weed district program after closing.

citations: Mont. Code Ann. Title 7, ch. 22, part 21 (County Noxious Weed Control Act)

title: Water Rights Disclosure and Ownership Update at Closing
description: Mont. Code Ann. § 85-2-424 requires that when a deed or other instrument transferring real property is presented for recording, the Realty Transfer Certificate must contain a water rights disclosure in which the transferor acknowledges whether any water rights are associated with the property and whether they will transfer with it. The buyer must update water right ownership with the Montana Department of Natural Resources and Conservation (DNRC) using Form 608 (Water Right Ownership Update) and pay the DNRC fee at closing or transfer; failure to pay the required fee can subject the transferee to a penalty. Water rights are a transferable property interest distinct from the land in Montana's prior-appropriation system.

required_actions.note: Transferor acknowledges on the Realty Transfer Certificate whether water rights exist and whether they transfer (Mont. Code Ann. § 85-2-424).
File DNRC Form 608 Water Right Ownership Update and pay the DNRC fee at closing; use Form 641 if water right interest is divided.

metadata.agency: Montana Department of Natural Resources and Conservation

title: Relationship (Agency) Disclosure Requirements
description: Mont. Code Ann. § 37-51-314 requires brokers and salespersons to disclose in writing the existence and nature of their agency or other relationships to the parties in a real estate transaction. A seller agent makes the initial disclosure to the seller when the listing agreement is executed; buyer agents disclose to buyers under written buyer broker agreements. A licensee may not act as a dual agent without the signed, written consent of both buyer and seller. Montana also recognizes the 'statutory broker' role (a licensee assisting without representing either party) under Mont. Code Ann. § 37-51-102.

required_actions.note: Written relationship disclosure to all parties; dual agency requires signed written consent of both buyer and seller (Mont. Code Ann. § 37-51-314).

title: No Transfer Tax — Realty Transfer Certificate Required for Recording
description: Montana imposes no real estate transfer tax or deed stamp tax. However, under the Realty Transfer Act, Mont. Code Ann. §§ 15-7-304 and 15-7-305, a completed Realty Transfer Certificate (Form RTC, a confidential tax document disclosing the sale price to the Department of Revenue for assessment purposes) must accompany any deed or instrument evidencing a transfer of real estate, and the county clerk and recorder may not accept the deed for recording without it. Willfully failing to file an accurate and complete certificate is punishable by a fine of up to $500, six months in jail, or both.

required_actions.note: File the completed Realty Transfer Certificate with the county clerk and recorder when presenting the deed for recording; includes the § 85-2-424 water rights disclosure section.
No transfer tax is due — the RTC is informational for Department of Revenue appraisal and is kept confidential.

citations: Mont. Code Ann. Title 15, ch. 7, part 3 (Realty Transfer Act)

title: Dry Funding State — Loan Proceeds Disbursed After Closing
description: Montana is classified by the mortgage industry as a dry funding state: it has no wet-settlement statute compelling same-day disbursement, so lenders may complete final review of the signed closing package before funding, and loan proceeds (and keys) are typically delivered days after the signing rather than at the closing table. Parties should set expectations accordingly — the transaction is not complete, and the seller is not paid, until the lender funds and the deed records. This is an industry classification rather than an affirmative statutory mandate; some lenders nonetheless fund same-day in practice.

required_actions.note: Advise buyer and seller that disbursement, recording, and possession may occur after the signing date; coordinate funding timeline with the lender and title company.
Confirm funding conditions and document-review turnaround with the lender before scheduling possession or move-in.

citations: Industry wet/dry funding classification — Montana has no wet-settlement statute (cf. Mont. Code Ann. Title 32)
Fannie Mae/industry settlement practice guides listing Montana as dry funding
